subject: system-design
title: Remote Procedure Calls (RPC)
summary: Calling a function that runs on another machine as if it were local — and why that 'as if' is the dangerous part.

blocks.text: An RPC lets one program invoke a function that actually runs on another machine. You write `getUser(id)` and call it like any other function, but the work happens on a remote server across the network. The goal is location transparency — the caller shouldn't need to know or care where the code runs.

The magic is in generated glue code called stubs. A client stub stands in for the remote function, and a server stub receives the call on the other side. Between them, arguments are serialized into bytes (marshalling), sent over the network, and deserialized back into values the server can use; the result makes the same trip home.

items: The client stub packs the arguments and sends a request.
The server stub unpacks them, runs the real function, and packs the result.
The client stub unpacks the result and hands it back to the caller.

blocks.text: REST models the world as resources you act on with HTTP verbs — GET a user, POST an order. RPC models it as actions you call — `createOrder`, `chargeCard`. RPC frameworks like gRPC use a compact binary format and a strict schema, which is fast and tightly typed; REST is more uniform, cacheable, and easy to inspect with ordinary HTTP tools.
A remote call is not a local call

The transparency is a useful illusion, but it leaks. A local call is fast and either succeeds or throws; a remote call adds network latency, can be lost in flight, and can fail partially — the server may have done the work even though you never got the reply. You also have to decide what a timeout means when the answer simply never arrives.

blocks.title: Don't treat remote as local
blocks.text: Assuming an RPC behaves like an in-process call is a classic mistake. Budget for latency, handle timeouts explicitly, and never assume that no response means the work didn't happen.

Because a request can fail after the server acted, clients retry — and a naive retry can charge a card twice. The fix is to make operations idempotent: running them again has the same effect as running them once, often via a client-supplied request id the server deduplicates. With idempotency, retries become safe instead of dangerous.

gRPC (Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2) and Apache Thrift are the workhorse RPC frameworks; both generate stubs from a schema so client and server stay in sync. Reach for RPC when you want typed, efficient service-to-service calls — but design as if the network is always between you, because it is.
